title: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy masquerading as peripartum cardiomyopathy
case_prompt:
A 49-year-old woman with a history of peripartum cardiomyopathy diagnosed in 2005 after her first pregnancy was referred for heart transplantation because of worsening heart failure. She reported chronic fatigue and dyspnea on exertion. Her medical history was notable for dual-chamber ICD implantation for primary prevention and subsequent appropriate ICD shocks for ventricular tachycardia. Despite optimal guideline-directed medical therapy, her left ventricular ejection fraction continued to decline. She had no history of pregnancy complications or family history of cardiomyopathy or sudden cardiac death.

On evaluation, electrocardiography showed atrial pacing, low-voltage QRS complexes, and left anterior fascicular block. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 16%, severe left ventricular hypokinesis, a left ventricular end-diastolic dimension of 58 mm, a left ventricular end-systolic dimension of 53 mm, moderate right ventricular dysfunction, moderate-to-severe right ventricular enlargement, severe tricuspid regurgitation, and an estimated right ventricular systolic pressure of 22 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary exercise testing demonstrated a peak oxygen consumption of 11.1 mL/kg/min (40% predicted). Coronary angiography showed normal coronary arteries. Laboratory evaluation was notable only for a creatinine level of 1.53 mg/dL.

Genetic testing for 81 cardiomyopathy‐related genes identified a variant of uncertain significance in exon 9 of the desmoplakin (DSP) gene, c.1045G>C (p.Ala349Pro). This variant was not present in population databases but had been observed in individuals with sudden cardiac death; in silico predictions of its effect were conflicting. Although she had biventricular cardiomyopathy on imaging and runs of ventricular tachycardia on device interrogation, she did not meet any of the 2010 Task Force diagnostic criteria for arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy. Six months after this evaluation, she underwent cardiac transplantation.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Peripartum cardiomyopathy considered — “Peripartum cardiomyopathy is usually a diagnosis of exclusion.”  
2. Dilated cardiomyopathy considered — “The differential diagnosis of heart failure around the time of pregnancy is broad and includes … dilated cardiomyopathy …”  
3. Stress cardiomyopathy considered — “The differential diagnosis of heart failure around the time of pregnancy is broad and includes … stress cardiomyopathy …”  
4. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy considered — “The differential diagnosis of heart failure around the time of pregnancy is broad and includes … hypertrophic cardiomyopathy …”  
5. Left ventricular noncompaction considered — “The differential diagnosis of heart failure around the time of pregnancy is broad and includes … left ventricular (LV) noncompaction …”  
6. Ischemic cardiomyopathy excluded — “Coronary angiography revealed normal coronary arteries.”  
7. ARVC initially excluded — “Although the patient had biventricular cardiomyopathy based on electrocardiography and echocardiography, she did not meet any of the 2010 Task Force diagnostic criteria of ARVC.”  
8. DSP gene VUS assessed — “This was a suspicious VUS given that it is not present in population databases but has been observed in individuals with sudden cardiac death.”  
9. ARVC confirmed pathologically — “Pathology features of the explanted heart were consistent with ARVC, including LV fibrofatty replacement in a midmural and subepicardial distribution … and RV near-total replacement by fibroadipose tissue with marked dilatation.”
